summary: Defines MIB objects for remote network monitoring (RMON) on high-speed networks, along with updated objects from the RMON-MIB. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: RMON is the part of SNMP for watching a network from a probe. The counters in the original RMON MIB are 32 bits wide, so on a fast link they wrap around and the totals become meaningless. This RFC adds a second set of tables with wider counters, and a counter that records how many times the old one wrapped.

questions: what is rmon high capacity mib
what is a counter64 in snmp
how does rmon handle counter overflow
subtitle: SNMP objects for RMON probes that add 64-bit and overflow counters so monitoring keeps up with fast networks.

tldr.problem: The RMON statistics counters of the original RMON and RMON-2 MIBs are 32 bits wide, which are not enough for the traffic volumes of high speed networks.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3273 defines the HC-RMON-MIB, a set of tables that sit alongside the existing RMON tables and add overflow counters and 64-bit counters. It also adds a media independent statistics table and extends three TopN rate-base enumerations.
tldr.outcome: A probe implements the groups it needs as units of conformance. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 4502.

today: RFC 3273 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2002 and has been updated by RFC 4502. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and the SNMP Framework
sections.content:
The SNMP Management Framework consists of five major components: an overall architecture, the mechanisms for describing and naming objects and events, the message protocols for transferring management information, the protocol operations for accessing that information, and a set of fundamental applications with a view-based access control mechanism.

Managed objects are accessed via a virtual information store, the Management Information Base, or MIB. Objects in the MIB are defined using the mechanisms defined in the Structure of Management Information. This memo specifies a MIB module that is compliant with SMIv2. A MIB conforming to SMIv1 can be produced through the appropriate translations, and the resulting translated MIB must be semantically equivalent, except where objects or events are omitted because no translation is possible, which is the case for Counter64.

This document continues the architecture created by the RMON MIB by supporting high speed networks. It defines objects for managing remote network monitoring devices, often called monitors or probes, which are instruments that exist for the purpose of managing a network. Often these remote probes are stand-alone devices that devote significant internal resources to the sole purpose of managing a network. An organization may employ many of these devices, one per network segment, and may also use them to give a network management service provider access to a client network, often geographically remote.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP lets a management program read counters from a device. The counters live in a MIB, a list of named values and tables that the device publishes. This RFC writes one more MIB module, in the modern SMIv2 form, and adds to two older ones.

sections.title: Overview and MIB Structure
sections.content:
The objects defined in this document are intended as an interface between an RMON agent and an RMON management application, and are not intended for direct manipulation by humans. While some users may tolerate the direct display of some of these objects, few will tolerate the complexity of manually manipulating objects to accomplish row creation. These functions should be handled by the management application.

Except for the mediaIndependentTable, each of the tables in this MIB adds high capacity capability to an associated table in the RMON-1 MIB or the RMON-2 MIB. The objects are arranged into fifteen groups: mediaIndependentGroup, etherStatsHighCapacityGroup, etherHistoryHighCapacityGroup, hostHighCapacityGroup, hostTopNHighCapacityGroup, matrixHighCapacityGroup, captureBufferHighCapacityGroup, protocolDistributionHighCapacityGroup, nlHostHighCapacityGroup, nlMatrixHighCapacityGroup, nlMatrixTopNHighCapacityGroup, alHostHighCapacityGroup, alMatrixHighCapacityGroup, alMatrixTopNHighCapacityGroup, and usrHistoryHighCapacityGroup.

These groups are the basic units of conformance. If a remote monitoring device implements a group, it must implement all the objects in that group. For example, a managed agent that implements the network layer matrix group must implement both the nlMatrixSDHighCapacityTable and the nlMatrixDSHighCapacityTable. Implementations of this MIB must also implement the system and interfaces group of MIB-II, which may also mandate the implementation of additional groups.

The groups provide a means of assigning object identifiers and a method for agent implementors to know which objects they must implement.
sections.plainLanguage: Each group of objects is a unit of conformance: a probe that supports one group has to support everything in it. The groups are named after the RMON table they extend, with HighCapacity added, so an implementor can tell at a glance what a probe does and does not offer.

sections.title: Updates to the RMON and RMON2 Objects
sections.content:
The document extends the enumerations in three objects from the RMON MIB and the RMON2 MIB, so that the same control object can choose between the old 32-bit table and the new high capacity table.

The hostTopNRateBase object in the RMON MIB originally had seven values, from hostTopNInPkts(1) to hostTopNOutMulticastPkts(7). The document adds hostTopNHCInPkts(8), hostTopNHCOutPkts(9), hostTopNHCInOctets(10) and hostTopNHCOutOctets(11). If the value is 7 or less, entries are created in the existing hostTopNTable; if it is 8 or more, entries are created in the hostTopNHighCapacityTable.

The nlMatrixTopNControlRateBase object in the RMON2 MIB originally had two values, nlMatrixTopNPkts(1) and nlMatrixTopNOctets(2). The document adds nlMatrixTopNHighCapacityPkts(3) and nlMatrixTopNHighCapacityOctets(4), with the same rule: a value of 2 or less uses the existing table, 3 or more uses the high capacity table.

The alMatrixTopNControlRateBase object in the RMON2 MIB originally had four values, from alMatrixTopNTerminalsPkts(1) to alMatrixTopNAllOctets(4). The document adds alMatrixTopNTerminalsHighCapacityPkts(5), alMatrixTopNTerminalsHighCapacityOctets(6), alMatrixTopNAllHighCapacityPkts(7) and alMatrixTopNAllHighCapacityOctets(8). The four high capacity values collect from all alMatrix entries, the same as the two all-protocol values they sit beside.
sections.plainLanguage: Three control objects get more choices, so that a manager can say whether it wants the old 32-bit counters or the new wide ones. The rule is simple: the lower numbers select the old table, the higher numbers select the high capacity table.

sections.title: Conventions for Good and Bad Packets
sections.content:
The conventions used throughout the RMON MIB and its companion documents are set out here.

Good packets are error-free packets that have a valid frame length. For example, on Ethernet, good packets are error-free packets that are between 64 octets long and 1518 octets long. They follow the form defined in the IEEE 802.3 specification.

Bad packets are packets that have proper framing and are therefore recognized as packets, but contain errors within the packet or have an invalid length. For example, on Ethernet, bad packets have a valid preamble and SFD, the Start of Frame Delimiter, but have a bad FCS, the Frame Check Sequence, or are either shorter than 64 octets or longer than 1518 octets.

The key words MUST, MUST NOT, REQUIRED, SHALL, SHALL NOT, SHOULD, SHOULD NOT, RECOMMENDED, MAY and OPTIONAL are to be interpreted as described in RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: The counters split traffic into good packets and bad packets. On Ethernet a good packet is error-free and between 64 and 1518 octets long. A bad packet is one the interface can recognise as a packet but that has errors inside it or the wrong length.

sections.title: The High Capacity Tables
sections.content:
The MIB module is called HC-RMON-MIB. Each high capacity table follows the same pattern. For every counter that the older MIB defines, the new table adds three objects: the old 32-bit counter itself, a 32-bit counter that records how many times the old one has overflowed, and a 64-bit counter that carries the real total.

The etherStatsHighCapacityTable is the clearest example. Its entry begins with etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts, a Counter32 counting the times the associated etherStatsPkts counter has overflowed, then etherStatsHighCapacityPkts, a Counter64 carrying the total number of packets received, then the same pair for octets. After that come the same pairs for packets of each length band: 64 octets, 65 to 127 octets, 128 to 255 octets, 256 to 511 octets, 512 to 1023 octets, and 1024 to 1518 octets.

The etherStatsHighCapacityOctets object also carries the formula for working out how busy a segment is. The result is a percentage on a scale of 0 to 100 percent, computed from the packet and octet counts sampled over an interval. The table is not appropriate for monitoring full-duplex Ethernet; for that, the utilization of the inbound path and of the outbound path are worked out separately from the mediaIndependentIn and mediaIndependentOut objects, and the utilization is the maximum of the two. That metric shows the amount of bandwidth left before congestion is experienced on the link.

The mediaIndependentTable is the one table that is not an extension of an older one. It collects utilization statistics for any media, including full and half duplex links and high capacity links. For half-duplex links, or full-duplex-capable links operating in half-duplex mode, the mediaIndependentIn objects are used and the mediaIndependentOut objects do not increment. For full-duplex links the mediaIndependentOut objects are present and increment. Whenever possible the probe should count packets moving away from the closest terminating equipment as output packets, and failing that, packets moving away from the DTE.

The captureBufferHighCapacityTable adds one object, captureBufferPacketHighCapacityTime, which gives the number of nanoseconds that had passed since the capture buffer was first turned on when a packet was captured, modulo 10^6. It is used together with the existing captureBufferPacketTime object, which holds milliseconds, so that the arrival time of a packet can be pinned down more precisely. The usrHistoryHighCapacityTable adds a user-defined collection of historical information from MIB objects on the probe, with scalability to statistics from high capacity networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Every high capacity table keeps three numbers for the same thing: the old 32-bit count, a count of how often that number wrapped around, and a 64-bit count that holds the true total. A manager reads the 64-bit figure and knows it is not going to roll over.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
In order to implement this MIB, a probe must capture all packets on the locally attached network, including packets between third parties. These packets are analyzed to collect network addresses, protocol usage information and conversation statistics. Data of this nature may be considered sensitive in some environments, and in such environments the administrator may wish to restrict SNMP access to the probe.

A probe implementing this MIB is likely to also implement RMON, which includes functions for returning the contents of captured packets, potentially including sensitive user data or passwords. It is recommended that SNMP access to these functions be restricted.

There are a number of management objects defined in this MIB that have a MAX-ACCESS clause of read-write or read-create. Such objects may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments, and support for SET operations in a non-secure environment without proper protection can have a negative effect on network operations.

SNMPv1 by itself is not a secure environment. Even if the network itself is secure, for example by using IPSec, there is no control as to who on the secure network is allowed to GET or SET the objects in this MIB. It is recommended that implementers consider the security features provided by the SNMPv3 framework, specifically the User-based Security Model and the View-based Access Control Model, and that it is then the responsibility of the customer or user to ensure that the SNMP entity giving access to an instance of this MIB is properly configured to give access only to those principals that have legitimate rights to read or change the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe has to see every packet on the segment, including traffic between other people, so the statistics it produces may be sensitive. The document says to restrict SNMP access to the probe, and to use the access controls of SNMPv3 rather than the older, unprotected SNMPv1.

sections.title: Conformance Statements
sections.content:
The conformance statements sit at the end of the MIB module in Section 5 of the document. They describe what a probe must implement to claim conformance to this MIB.

The module defines a Media Independent compliance statement whose mandatory groups are the mediaIndependentGroup and the hcRMONInformationGroup. The hcRMONInformationGroup holds a single object, hcRMONCapabilities, which is an indication of the high capacity RMON groups supported on at least one interface by the probe.

The High Capacity RMON-1 compliance statement makes the groups optional but ties each to the older group it extends. The etherStatsHighCapacityGroup is optional but requires the rmonEtherStatsGroup. The etherHistoryHighCapacityGroup is optional but requires the rmonHistoryControlGroup and the rmonEthernetHistoryGroup. The hostHighCapacityGroup is mandatory when the hostTopNHighCapacityGroup is implemented, and also requires the rmonHostGroup. The hostTopNHighCapacityGroup is optional but requires the rmonHostTopNGroup. The matrixHighCapacityGroup is optional but requires the rmonMatrixGroup. The captureBufferHighCapacityGroup is optional but requires the rmonFilterGroup and the rmonPacketCaptureGroup. The RMON Ethernet Statistics Group is mandatory if the etherStatsHighCapacityGroup is implemented, the RMON History Control Group is mandatory if the etherHistoryHighCapacityGroup is implemented, the RMON Ethernet History Group is mandatory if the etherHistoryHighCapacityGroup is implemented, and the rmon1EnhancementGroup is mandatory for systems which implement RMON.

Separate compliance statements cover the High Capacity RMON-2 MIB and the High Capacity RMON-2 Application Layer MIB, with the same pattern of dependency on the older groups.
sections.plainLanguage: A probe can pick and choose the high capacity groups it offers, but each one drags in the older group it extends. So a probe that claims to count Ethernet packets at full width has to keep the original Ethernet statistics group working as well.

items.label: hostTopNHCInPkts
items.desc: Added by this RFC. Selects the high capacity table.

viz.caption: THE THREE OBJECTS BEHIND EACH HIGH CAPACITY COUNTER

items.title: The old counter
items.text: The 32-bit counter from the earlier MIB. It still exists and still counts.

items.title: The overflow counter
items.text: A 32-bit count of how many times the old counter has wrapped around.

items.title: The wide counter
items.text: A 64-bit counter that carries the real total, so it does not wrap.

viz.caption: THE ETHERSTATS HIGH CAPACITY ENTRY, AS WRITTEN IN THE RFC

data.title: EtherStatsHighCapacityEntry
data.code:
EtherStatsHighCapacityEntry ::= SEQUENCE {
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts                 Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts                         Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowOctets               Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOctets                       Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts64Octets         Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts64Octets                 Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts65to127Octets    Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts65to127Octets            Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts128to255Octets   Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts128to255Octets           Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts256to511Octets   Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts256to511Octets           Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts512to1023Octets  Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts512to1023Octets          Counter64,
    etherStatsHighCapacityOverflowPkts1024to1518Octets Counter32,
    etherStatsHighCapacityPkts1024to1518Octets         Counter64
}
